old.name: Sainte-Chapelle
old.hook: Louis IX's royal chapel, consecrated on 26 April 1248 and raised in well under a decade to house Christ's Crown of Thorns. The upper chapel's windows rise some 15 metres — roughly 1,113 stained-glass scenes — so that the stone almost disappears and you stand inside a lantern of light.

The upper chapel's windows rise some 15 metres — roughly 1,113 stained-glass scenes — so that the stone almost disappears and you stand inside a lantern of light. Signal 8 Bd du Palais, 4e (Île de la Cité). Daily from 9:00 (to 19:00 Apr-Sep, 17:00 Oct-Mar). Since a two-tier fare began on 12 Jan 2026, about EUR 22 for non-EEA visitors and EUR 16 for EEA residents; free for under-18s and EU nationals aged 18-25, and free for all on the 1st Sunday of the month Nov-Mar. Book a timed slot online and expect airport-style security — it shares the gate with the working law courts.

old.name: Palais Garnier
old.hook: Charles Garnier's opera house, inaugurated 1875 and the temple of Second Empire excess: the marble grand staircase, gilt and mirrors, Marc Chagall's dreamlike 1964 ceiling over the auditorium, and the underground water reservoir that gave Leroux his Phantom.
old.text: Charles Garnier's opera house, inaugurated 1875 and the temple of Second Empire excess: the marble grand staircase, gilt and mirrors, Marc Chagall's dreamlike 1964 ceiling over the auditorium, and the underground water reservoir that gave Leroux his Phantom. Signal Place de l'Opéra, 9e. Self-guided daily from 10:00; last entry an hour before the 16:00 close (open to 17:00 from mid-July to end of August). Since 2026, roughly EUR 15 for EEA-resident adults, EUR 25 for non-EEA; under-12 free. Auditorium access is never guaranteed — rehearsals close it without notice. Free audio tour on the Paris Opera app, or simply book a ballet/opera night.

old.name: Bourse de Commerce — Pinault Collection
old.hook: Paris's 18th-century grain exchange under its later iron-and-glass dome — the commodities floor at the edge of Zola's 'belly of Paris', Les Halles — reopened in 2021 as François Pinault's contemporary-art museum, with a raw concrete cylinder dropped inside the rotunda by Tadao Ando.

Signal 2 rue de Viarmes, 1er. EUR 15, EUR 10 reduced (18-26), under-18 free; free the 1st Saturday of the month 17:00-21:00. Open 11:00-19:00, Fridays to 21:00, closed Tuesdays. E. Dehillerin is a two-minute walk — pair the art with the copper.

old.name: Musee Rodin
old.label: 7th arrondissement
old.hook: The 18th-century Hotel Biron sits in roughly three hectares of formal grounds: some 2,000 rose bushes of about 100 varieties frame the house, with gravel walks and clipped box beyond. The Thinker broods on his plinth among the box trees, The Gates of Hell rises at the far end, and Rodin's bronze and marble stand under open sky. Indoors the collection is Rodin's own -- The Kiss, the studies, the Camille Claudel room.
old.text: The 18th-century Hotel Biron sits in roughly three hectares of formal grounds: some 2,000 rose bushes of about 100 varieties frame the house, with gravel walks and clipped box beyond. The Thinker broods on his plinth among the box trees, The Gates of Hell rises at the far end, and Rodin's bronze and marble stand under open sky. Indoors the collection is Rodin's own -- The Kiss, the studies, the Camille Claudel room. This is the one everyone means when they say a museum should come with a garden. You can buy a garden-only ticket and spend a whole afternoon walking the rose alleys with The Thinker for company, the golden dome of Les Invalides over the wall. The garden café L'Augustine, the garden cafe-restaurant set within the sculpture park not far from The Thinker (long known simply as the Cafe du Musee Rodin) -- a small interior salon that spills onto terrace tables in good weather, open Tuesday to Sunday. Anchor Hotel Biron, built between 1727 and 1732 to designs by architect Jean Aubert (with Jacques Gabriel); Rodin took studios here from 1908, and it opened as his museum on 4 August 1919.

old.name: Musee de la Vie Romantique
old.label: 9th arrondissement
old.hook: A green-shuttered villa of 1830 reached down a cobbled alley, once the home of painter Ary Scheffer -- rose bushes, clematis and bellflowers around a little glass conservatory. The collection gathers George Sand keepsakes on the ground floor (furniture, jewellery, a cast of her arm) and Scheffer's Romantic canvases upstairs.
old.text: A green-shuttered villa of 1830 reached down a cobbled alley, once the home of painter Ary Scheffer -- rose bushes, clematis and bellflowers around a little glass conservatory. The collection gathers George Sand keepsakes on the ground floor (furniture, jewellery, a cast of her arm) and Scheffer's Romantic canvases upstairs. It feels like stepping out of the city into a country cottage. Scheffer held his Friday salons in these rooms, and Chopin, Delacroix and George Sand walked this same garden. The house and its tea salon reopened in February 2026 after a refurbishment. The garden café Rose Bakery salon de the, set in the garden's glass greenhouse and on the leafy terrace, serving scones, cakes and savoury tarts; open Tuesday to Sunday through the year. Anchor Hotel Scheffer-Renan, built 1830, the studio-home of Dutch-born Romantic painter Ary Scheffer (1795-1858); free municipal museum.

old_also.name: Musée de la Vie Romantique
old_also.hook: A green-shuttered 1830 villa at the end of a cobbled courtyard, once a painter's house, now a museum of the Romantic era — with a rose-garden tea salon.
old_also.text: A green-shuttered 1830 villa at the end of a cobbled courtyard, once a painter's house, now a museum of the Romantic era — with a rose-garden tea salon. This was the home of the Dutch-born Romantic painter Ary Scheffer, who moved to rue Chaptal in 1830 and, with his household, held Friday-evening salons that drew the whole 'Nouvelle Athènes' quarter — Chopin, Delacroix, Pauline Viardot and George Sand, who lived minutes away. Sand never lived here but came often, and the museum keeps her jewellery, plaster casts and mementoes. It reopened on 14 February 2026 after a restoration begun in September 2024. One real thing: the garden tea salon is a secret to Parisians, open without a museum ticket, not just a museum add-on. Signal Ary Scheffer's 1830 house; reopened 14 February 2026 after restoration

old.name: Musee de Montmartre - Jardins Renoir
old.label: 18th arrondissement
old.hook: The oldest house on the hill -- a 17th-century manor -- with three terraced gardens named for Renoir, looking over the Clos Montmartre vineyard. The collection tells the story of bohemian Montmartre: Toulouse-Lautrec, the Chat Noir, and Suzanne Valadon's reconstructed studio.
old.text: The oldest house on the hill -- a 17th-century manor -- with three terraced gardens named for Renoir, looking over the Clos Montmartre vineyard. The collection tells the story of bohemian Montmartre: Toulouse-Lautrec, the Chat Noir, and Suzanne Valadon's reconstructed studio. Renoir rented rooms here and painted the Bal du Moulin de la Galette and The Swing (La Balancoire) in these very gardens -- you sit where the pictures were made, above the last working vines in Paris. The garden café Cafe Renoir, tucked into the gardens overlooking the vineyard, open Wednesday to Sunday (a 6-euro garden-and-cafe ticket lets you in even without the full museum). Anchor 12 rue Cortot, a 17th-century house; Renoir had a studio here in 1875-1876, and Valadon and Utrillo later worked in the building.

old.name: Musée Nissim de Camondo
old.hook: A 1910s mansion built as a shrine to 18th-century French decorative arts — and, unavoidably, to one family's annihilation.
old.text: A 1910s mansion built as a shrine to 18th-century French decorative arts — and, unavoidably, to one family's annihilation. Count Moïse de Camondo, from a great Sephardic banking family, built this house (1911–14) modelled on the Petit Trianon to hold his Marie-Antoinette-era furniture and Sèvres. He named it for his son Nissim, a French airman killed in 1917, and left it to the nation as a museum, opened in 1936. Years later his daughter Béatrice, her ex-husband and their two children were deported and murdered at Auschwitz — the family ended entirely. HONEST FLAG: the museum has been closed for renovation since 4 August 2024 and is announced to reopen only in early 2027, so it cannot be visited in 2026 — hold it for a return trip, and take Jacquemart-André (above) instead for now. Signal Opened 1936; CLOSED for renovation since 4 August 2024, reopening announced early 2027 — not visitable in 2026

old_also.name: Musee Nissim de Camondo
old_also.label: 8th arrondissement
old_also.hook: A mansion built in 1911-1914 in the manner of Versailles' Petit Trianon, its rear rooms and formal garden opening onto Parc Monceau. Inside, a perfectly preserved collection of 18th-century French decorative arts -- panelling, furniture, Sevres porcelain, silver.
old_also.text: A mansion built in 1911-1914 in the manner of Versailles' Petit Trianon, its rear rooms and formal garden opening onto Parc Monceau. Inside, a perfectly preserved collection of 18th-century French decorative arts -- panelling, furniture, Sevres porcelain, silver. A frozen aristocratic house with a heartbreaking story: Moise de Camondo named it for his son Nissim, an aviator killed in the First World War, and left it to the nation; the surviving family was later murdered at Auschwitz. The garden over the park is part of the hush. The garden café No cafe in the house; Parc Monceau lies directly beyond the garden windows for a break. Anchor Hotel Moise de Camondo, built 1911-1914 by architect Rene Sergent with a garden by landscape architect Achille Duchene; opened as a museum in 1936.

old.name: Musée Jacquemart-André
old.hook: A Second-Empire mansion kept as its owners left it — a private house stuffed with Italian Renaissance masters, a rococo double staircase, and a frescoed tea room.
old.text: A Second-Empire mansion kept as its owners left it — a private house stuffed with Italian Renaissance masters, a rococo double staircase, and a frescoed tea room. It was the home of banker Édouard André and the society painter Nélie Jacquemart — who first met him by painting his portrait, then married him — and together they filled it with Botticelli, Uccello and Tiepolo on annual buying trips to Italy. Bequeathed to the Institut de France, it reopened on 6 September 2024 after a €6.5-million restoration. This is the open, near-identical companion to the Camondo house nearby (see below): a plutocrat's private collection frozen in place. The real thing: don't skip the café — the tea room 'Le Nélie', in the former dining room, sits under a genuine Tiepolo ceiling. Signal Home of Édouard André & Nélie Jacquemart; reopened 6 September 2024 after €6.5M restoration

old.name: Musée Gustave Moreau
old.hook: The house-and-studio the Symbolist painter Gustave Moreau turned into his own museum, crammed with some 1,300 paintings, watercolours and drawings and reached by a theatrical iron spiral staircase.
old.text: The house-and-studio the Symbolist painter Gustave Moreau turned into his own museum, crammed with some 1,300 paintings, watercolours and drawings and reached by a theatrical iron spiral staircase. Late in life, Moreau decided his home should become a museum of his work, and had the upper floors rebuilt into vast top-lit studios linked by a swirling wrought-iron spiral stair — a stage set for his jewelled, mythological canvases. He died in 1898 and the museum opened in 1903, almost untouched since. It is one of Paris's great 'not-obvious' museums, hidden on a quiet 9th-arrondissement street. The real thing to grasp: the pictures are hung frame-to-frame, floor to ceiling, as Moreau intended — an overwhelming density you won't see in any conventional gallery. Signal Painter's own house-museum; opened 1903 with its famous spiral staircase

old.name: Galerie Vivienne & Passage des Panoramas
old.hook: Two of Paris's surviving 19th-century glass-roofed shopping arcades — mosaic-floored Vivienne and the older, scruffier Panoramas — a few minutes apart.
old.text: Two of Paris's surviving 19th-century glass-roofed shopping arcades — mosaic-floored Vivienne and the older, scruffier Panoramas — a few minutes apart. The covered passages were the ancestors of the department store: gaslit, weatherproof lanes of shops built when the streets were mud. The Passage des Panoramas is among the oldest, cut through in 1799 by an American shipowner, James Thayer, to link two rotundas showing 'panorama' paintings — and in 1817 it became the first Paris passage to be lit by gas. Galerie Vivienne (built 1823, opened 1826) is the grand one, a neo-classical arcade of mosaic floors and half-moon windows, still holding a famous antiquarian bookshop and old-world shopfronts. The real thing: of the dozens that once existed only about twenty remain — these two, walkable together, are the pair to see. Signal Passage des Panoramas cut through 1799 (gas-lit from 1817); Galerie Vivienne built 1823

old_also.name: Passage des Panoramas
old_also.hook: The oldest of Paris's glass-roofed covered passages, opened 1800 — an ancestor of the shopping arcade. The celebrated engraver Stern settled here in 1834 and the storefront survives; today it's a tight run of stamp and postcard dealers and pocket-sized bistros.
old_also.text: The oldest of Paris's glass-roofed covered passages, opened 1800 — an ancestor of the shopping arcade. The celebrated engraver Stern settled here in 1834 and the storefront survives; today it's a tight run of stamp and postcard dealers and pocket-sized bistros. Signal Entrances at 11 Bd Montmartre and rue Saint-Marc, 2e. Free, open roughly 6:00 to midnight daily. String it together with Galerie Vivienne nearby and Passage Jouffroy directly across the boulevard for an hour out of the rain.

old.name: Musée de la Chasse et de la Nature
old.hook: A pair of Marais mansions turned into a witty, unsettling cabinet of curiosities on the human-animal relationship — taxidermy, arms, and contemporary art in panelled salons.
old.text: A pair of Marais mansions turned into a witty, unsettling cabinet of curiosities on the human-animal relationship — taxidermy, arms, and contemporary art in panelled salons. It occupies the 17th-century Hôtel de Guénégaud — the only surviving private mansion built by architect François Mansart — and the neighbouring Hôtel de Mongelas, run by the Fondation François Sommer. Far from a dusty hunting collection, it stages animals and objects like an art installation — a room with a ceiling of owl feathers, a boar peering from a cabinet — which is why designers and art crowds treat it as a Marais secret. The real thing to know: it is a museum with a sense of humour and staging, closer to a Wunderkammer than a natural-history hall — and blessedly uncrowded. Signal In the Hôtel de Guénégaud, the only surviving private mansion by François Mansart; run by the Fondation François Sommer

old.name: Grande Mosquee de Paris - tea garden
old.label: 5th arrondissement
old.hook: Not a museum but a Hispano-Moorish mosque of the 1920s whose cafe maure opens a tiled patio garden to anyone, no ticket needed -- fig trees, a fountain, blue-and-white zellige, sparrows in the plane trees.
old.text: Not a museum but a Hispano-Moorish mosque of the 1920s whose cafe maure opens a tiled patio garden to anyone, no ticket needed -- fig trees, a fountain, blue-and-white zellige, sparrows in the plane trees. Mint tea poured tall and sweet, gazelle-horn pastries, the shade of the fig trees -- one of the most transporting corners in the Latin Quarter. (A working place of worship with a public tea garden, not a museum in the strict sense.) The garden café The Cafe Maure / salon de the itself, open daily, serving mint tea and North African pastries around the patio. Anchor Built 1922-1926 in Hispano-Moorish style and inaugurated in 1926, raised in homage to the Muslim soldiers who died for France in the First World War.
